lockFileMaintenance.description: config:recommended leaves this off, which would freeze every transitive dependency forever: caret requirements in Cargo.toml stay satisfied by the committed Cargo.lock, so nothing else refreshes it. CI runs --locked, so the lockfile is what ships. Two local overrides, both required: minimumReleaseAge must be nulled because these PRs are synthesized with no release timestamp, and renovate's default timestamp-required behaviour would hold them pending forever with no error to notice. Nulling it is also honest — the refresh shells out to `cargo update`, which has no release-age awareness, so the top-level cooldown could never have applied here. automerge is off for the same reason: this is the one path where a freshly-published or later-yanked release reaches main ungated, and that hazard compiles and passes tests, so CI cannot stand in for the cooldown.

vulnerabilityAlerts.description: The 7-day cooldown exists to dodge yanked releases; applying it to a published advisory would delay the fix for exactly as long as the exposure lasts.

packageRules.description: 0.x crates: under Cargo's semver rules 0.6 -> 0.7 is a breaking change, but renovate classifies it as `minor`, so without this rule it would ride in the grouped batch above. Un-grouped for the same reason as majors: isolate the break. Must stay after the grouping rule to win.

0.0.x crates are a separate case: every 0.0.x -> 0.0.y is breaking under Cargo's rules, yet renovate classifies it as `patch`, which the grouping rule above would swallow. Covers both types so the classification cannot route around it.
Major updates: one PR per package. A major usually breaks the API surface, so isolating each keeps the break cheap to diagnose. Automerge stays on — CI is the gate.

Rust compiler: its own PR. A bump lands new default-on clippy lints across the whole crate at once (see rust-toolchain.toml), which under -D warnings breaks CI on code that never changed. Last rule wins — keep this LAST.
